full_text:
Long update post. Short version at the bottom if you want to save time.

So, what's next for @KurosunCo? Let's start with the Shogun. It's a smooth control pad with a very consistent and pleasant surface. Has great performance all around. We made some key upgrades to the construction, starting with the base being thicker and more dense feeling, so it has heft to it and feels very solid. The rebound properties are also drastically better than any of our previous releases. This is due to the new 2nd gen Alpha Cell, we will be the first to use it, and as always we will have our custom version of it. This new generation performs more consistently and solves all the issues of previous alpha cell. Combined with the added 1mm thickness to the base, we have a really solid foundation now, sitting in between a soft and a mid for a perfect blend of consistency and comfort. With that, the stitching was also improved. Not only is it tighter, it now sits under the surface. The Shogun is expected to be ready before December.

We've also implemented rigorous QC to all Kurosun products, starting with the Shogun. It will be our highest quality release yet in terms of QC and attention to detail, as well as the construction of the product.

Following this trend, the new Samurai "1.5" will release later after the Shogun, and it'll be based on the same improvements and principles. The same thick new gen 2 base, the improved stitching, and the improved construction. But there's more than just those changes, Samurai 1.5 is actually getting a change to how the surface is processed and treated, resulting in a much smoother feel and also more consistent across the x/y axes. More notably, though, is that Samurai 1.5 is actually much faster in glide speed, rivaling surfaces that would normally be considered "speed" mousepads. So the Samurai will be undergoing some fundamental changes. We expect this one to be ready by late January.

To make this new Samurai make sense in our lineup, Ninja 1.5 (again based on the same exact principles and improvements) will become even faster and more durable to maintain its position as our fastest offering. This one is still being worked on and perfected and will likely only drop around March of 2025.

Short version: there are no shortcuts, read the full post above🙂

full_text:
I think there is a part of business that is rarely talked about. It's the cost of goods, and how even a simple run of a few thousand units (which is usually the minimum required) can accumulate quickly for each product. These are an example of just two products. 

It also doesn't include shipping, marketing, artwork, animation, website, payroll etc, these are just the raw production costs and nothing else.

Well, why does it matter? Because sometimes someone asks "can you just make x product or make this colorway?". Each product like that in my case can easily surpass $200,000-250,000 when you combine all the costs. It takes very careful consideration and planning.

In the case of Hana, we took pre-orders, which helped. But we've rarely ever done pre-orders, and I don't think we'll do them again. I hate the waiting process. I'd rather take the risk and just produce a certain amount.

Anyways, this is just a small insight into one part of this business that I thought was interesting, and may help some people realize that it's not as easy as "why not just make this?"

full_text:
So, what's up with the unexpectedly super-fast GLSSWRKS Polarity Series?

Quick explainer:

Glass pads have a factory tolerance for surface roughness (Ra) where lower number = smoother.

• Hana had a target Ra of 1.0 (±0.25).

• Polarity Series aimed higher with a tighter tolerance of ±0.15.

Our batch overshot this mark, landing at an Ra of 2.0-2.2. This increased texture makes the pads noticeably faster, a surprise twist that's actually kinda awesome for speed enthusiasts. This is why I want to repurpose it into a very unique and ultra-fast pad 'by tekkusai'.

full_text:
Most peripherals roll out of the same handful of factories.

Only two or three plants handle nearly every glass or cloth mousepad, plus a good chunk of keyboards and mice. Two solution providers supply almost all mouse firmware.

So the assembly site alone tells you almost nothing about a product. That is just the final step.

What matters is the materials and the work that happens first. Choosing the right glass, sourcing the right fabric, and perfecting a custom mouse shape that actually took thought and effort.

You could walk through Wooting’s factory today, but without their software and firmware you leave with nothing useful.

That’s why my philosophy going forward is to put my time and money into sourcing and R&D. The goal is custom, well-considered products that speak for themselves.
